pumac-2016-team-01.title: Similar triangles
pumac-2016-team-01.body:
Set $AB=a$, $BC=b$, $AC=c$, so $a^2+b^2=c^2$. Since $\angle ABC=\angle BAD=90^\circ$, $AD\parallel BC$, so $\angle CAD=\angle ACB$. Right triangles $ABC$ and $DCA$ (right angles at $B$ and $C$) are therefore similar, giving $AD=\frac{c^2}{b}$ and $CD=\frac{ca}{b}$. We need $AD$, $CD$ to be integers with $(a,b,c)$ a Pythagorean triple.

The triple $(a,b,c)=(12,9,15)$ gives $AD=\frac{225}9=25$ and $CD=\frac{15\cdot12}{9}=20$. Since $AD>AC=c$, a smaller $AD$ would force $c<25$, and checking all Pythagorean triples with $c<25$ shows none has $b\mid c^2$ and $b\mid ca$ with a smaller $c^2/b$. So the minimum is $25$.

**Answer: 25**

pumac-2016-team-02.title: Tangent lines from a tower
pumac-2016-team-02.body:
By symmetry the towers are spaced $30^\circ$ apart, so each must see $15^\circ$ of the equator on either side. A tower of height $h$ sees the point at angle $\theta$ (central angle) exactly when the line of sight is tangent: $\cos\theta=\frac{1000}{1000+h}$. With $\theta=15^\circ$ and $\cos15^\circ=\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}$,
$$1+\frac h{1000}=\frac4{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}=\sqrt6-\sqrt2,$$
so $h=1000\sqrt6-1000\sqrt2-1000$ and $a+b+c+d+e=1000+6+1000+2+1000=3008$.

**Answer: 3008**

pumac-2016-team-03.title: Case on the largest prime factor
pumac-2016-team-03.body:
$n$ must share a prime with each of $\{2,11,19\}$, $\{3,13,17\}$, $\{5,11,13\}$, $\{7,17,19\}$.

- If $19\mid n$: $\frac n{19}$ must share a factor with both $3\cdot13\cdot17$ and $5\cdot11\cdot13$, so $n\ge19\cdot13>200$: impossible.
- If $17\mid n$: $\frac n{17}\le11$ must share a factor with both $2\cdot11\cdot19$ and $5\cdot11\cdot13$: $\frac n{17}\in\{10,11\}$, giving $170$ and $187$.
- If $13\mid n$ (and not $17,19$): $\frac n{13}$ must meet $2\cdot11\cdot19$ and $7\cdot17\cdot19$, so it is divisible by $2$ and $7$: $n=13\cdot14=182$.
- If none of $13,17,19$ divide $n$: then $3$ and $7$ divide $n$ (to hit the 2nd and 4th sets), and $n$ must also meet the 1st and 3rd sets, forcing $\frac n{21}\ge10$, i.e. $n>200$: impossible.

Sum: $170+182+187=539$.

**Answer: 539**

pumac-2016-team-05.title: Least common multiple of cycle lengths
pumac-2016-team-05.body:
$n(f)$ is the order of the permutation, the lcm of its cycle lengths, which sum to $16$. Only prime powers matter (a composite cycle length can be split into prime-power cycles without lowering the lcm). Casework on the largest prime-power cycle: $13\Rightarrow13\cdot3=39$; $11\Rightarrow11\cdot3\cdot2=66$; $9\Rightarrow9\cdot5\cdot2=90$; $8\Rightarrow8\cdot5\cdot3=120$; $7\Rightarrow7\cdot5\cdot4=140$ (cycles $7+5+4=16$). The maximum is $140$.

**Answer: 140**

pumac-2016-team-06.title: Recurrence on bit-strings
pumac-2016-team-06.body:
Numbers below $100$ with no two adjacent $1$s in binary are exactly the $7$-bit strings (leading zeros allowed) with no adjacent $1$s, since every $7$-bit number $\ge96$ starts with $11$.

Let $N(d)$ be the number of valid $d$-bit strings ($N=1,2,3,5,8,13,21,34$ for $d=0,\dots,7$) and $A(d)$ the sum of their values. A string ending in $0$ has twice the value of its first $d-1$ bits; a string ending in $1$ must end in $01$, with value $4x+1$ for a valid $(d-2)$-bit prefix $x$. So $A(d)=2A(d-1)+4A(d-2)+N(d-2)$, with $A(0)=0$, $A(1)=1$. This gives $A(2)=3$, $A(3)=12$, $A(4)=39$, $A(5)=131$, $A(6)=426$, $A(7)=1389$.

**Answer: 1389**

pumac-2016-team-07.title: Radical axis
pumac-2016-team-07.body:
Triangles $AHT$ and $BHS$ are right-angled at $T$ and $S$, so $O$ is the midpoint of $AH$ and $P$ the midpoint of $BH$; hence $HO=\frac{11}2$, $HP=3$ and $OP=\frac{AB}{2}=7$ (midline of triangle $HAB$).

The common chord $GH$ is perpendicular to the line of centers $OP$, so $X$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $H$ to $OP$. Then $XO^2-XP^2=(HO^2-HX^2)-(HP^2-HX^2)=HO^2-HP^2=\frac{121}{4}-9=\frac{85}{4}$. With $X$ between $O$ and $P$, $XO+XP=7$, so $XO-XP=\frac{85/4}{7}=\frac{85}{28}$ and $m+n=113$ (confirmed by coordinates).

**Answer: 113**

pumac-2016-team-08.title: Linearity of expectation
pumac-2016-team-08.body:
$\sum b_i^2$ equals the sum over balls of the number of balls (including itself) in that ball's bucket. For one ball the expected number is $1+99\cdot\frac1{10}=\frac{109}{10}$. By linearity, the answer is $100\cdot\frac{109}{10}=1090$.

**Answer: 1090**

pumac-2016-team-09.title: Reflect across the bisector
pumac-2016-team-09.body:
$AC=\sqrt{16+25}=\sqrt{41}$. The incenter and the $A$-excenter both lie on the bisector of $\angle A$. $BI$ and $BE$ are the internal and external bisectors at $B$, so $\angle IBE=90^\circ$; similarly $\angle ICE=90^\circ$. Hence $B$ and $C$ lie on the circle with diameter $IE$, whose center is on line $AI$. Reflection in $AI$ preserves this circle and swaps lines $AC$ and $AB$, so it sends $C$ to a point of the circle on line $AB$: either $B$ or $D$. Since $AB\ne AC$ it is $D$, so $AD=AC=\sqrt{41}$ and $BD=\sqrt{41}-4$. Therefore $a+b=45$ (confirmed with coordinates).

**Answer: 45**

pumac-2016-team-10.title: Open boxes early, not late
pumac-2016-team-10.body:
Working backwards over the six time slots (a dynamic program, which I also ran to confirm), Chad should open a new box only when at least 4 slots remain (opening in slot 4 gives expected gain exactly $0$, so it can be skipped). So: in the first three slots, whenever a customer comes and no candy is open, he opens a box; in the last three slots he never opens a box, only sells what is left.

Let $k$ be the number of the first three customers who choose Chad ($k=0,1,2,3$ with probabilities $\frac18,\frac38,\frac38,\frac18$), and let $j\sim\text{Bin}(3,\frac12)$ be the number among the last three.
- $k=0$: profit $0$.
- $k=1$: one box opened, one candy sold, $2$ left: profit $-1.5+1.5\min(j,2)$; equals $1.5$ if $j\ge2$ (prob. $\frac12$), $0$ if $j=1$, $-1.5$ if $j=0$ (prob. $\frac18$). Expected $\frac12\cdot1.5-\frac18\cdot1.5=\frac9{16}$.
- $k=2$: one box, two sold, one left: profit $1.5$ if $j\ge1$, else $0$: expected $\frac78\cdot1.5=\frac{21}{16}$.
- $k=3$: one box fully sold: profit $1.5$.

Expected profit: $\frac38\cdot\frac9{16}+\frac38\cdot\frac{21}{16}+\frac18\cdot\frac32=\frac{57}{64}$. So $m+n=121$.

**Answer: 121**

pumac-2016-team-11.title: Expected maximum
pumac-2016-team-11.body:
Given $a+b+c=1$, $(a,b,c)$ is uniform on the simplex, and $d$ is independent and uniform on $[0,1]$. So $P(d>\max(a,b,c))=1-E[\max(a,b,c)]$.

Compute $E[\max]=3\cdot E[a;\ a\text{ is the max}]$. If $a<\frac12$ (and is the max): the region has probability $\frac1{12}$ with mean $a=\frac49$; if $a>\frac12$ (automatically the max): probability $\frac14$ with mean $\frac23$. So $E[\max]=3\left(\frac1{12}\cdot\frac49+\frac14\cdot\frac23\right)=\frac{11}{18}$.

(Equivalently the expected largest of three spacings of $[0,1]$ is $\frac13\left(1+\frac12+\frac13\right)=\frac{11}{18}$.)

The probability is $1-\frac{11}{18}=\frac7{18}$, so $m+n=25$.

**Answer: 25**

pumac-2016-team-12.title: A harmonic-type operation
pumac-2016-team-12.body:
Define $a\star b=\frac{ab-1}{a+b-2}$. Then $a\star b-1=\frac{ab-a-b+1}{a+b-2}=\frac{(a-1)(b-1)}{(a-1)+(b-1)}$, so $\frac1{a\star b-1}=\frac1{a-1}+\frac1{b-1}$. In terms of $u=\frac1{a-1}$ the operation is just addition, hence it does not matter in which order numbers are combined:
$$\frac1{S(n)-1}=\sum_{k=2}^n\frac1{k^2-1}=\frac12\sum_{k=2}^n\left(\frac1{k-1}-\frac1{k+1}\right)\longrightarrow\frac12\left(1+\frac12\right)=\frac34.$$
Thus $r=1+\frac43=\frac73$ and $m+n=10$.

**Answer: 10**

pumac-2016-team-13.title: Cut corners off a tetrahedron
pumac-2016-team-13.body:
The six points lie on the six edges of the tetrahedron $A_1=(0,0,0)$, $A_2=(10,0,0)$, $A_3=(4,6,0)$, $A_4=(8,2,8)$, of volume $\frac16\cdot10\cdot6\cdot8=80$: $(x,0,0)$ on $A_1A_2$, $(2x,3x,0)$ on $A_1A_3$, $(0,0,0)=A_1$ on $A_1A_4$, $(7,3,0)$ the midpoint of $A_2A_3$, $(9,1,4)$ the midpoint of $A_2A_4$, and $(5,5,2)$ on $A_3A_4$ at $\frac14$ of the way from $A_3$. The polyhedron is the tetrahedron with the four corners cut off; a corner cut at fractions $p,q,r$ along the three edges has volume $80pqr$.

- At $A_1$: fractions $\frac x{10},\frac x2,0$: volume $0$.
- At $A_2$: fractions $\frac{10-x}{10},\frac12,\frac12$: volume $20\cdot\frac{10-x}{10}$, expectation $19$.
- At $A_3$: fractions $\frac{2-x}{2},\frac12,\frac14$: volume $5(2-x)$, expectation $\frac{15}{2}$.
- At $A_4$: fractions $1,\frac12,\frac34$: volume $30$.

Expected volume $=80-0-19-\frac{15}{2}-30=\frac{47}{2}$, so $m+n=49$. (A direct computation of the hull volume as a function of $x$ confirms it is linear with average $\frac{47}2$.)

**Answer: 49**

pumac-2016-team-14.title: Compare the top two coefficients
pumac-2016-team-14.body:
Write $n=2016$ and $a=a_{2015}$. Then $P(2x+1)=2^nx^n+2^{n-1}(n+a)x^{n-1}+\cdots$, so the coefficient of $x^{2n-1}$ in $P(x)P(2x+1)$ is $2^na+2^{n-1}(n+a)$.

Since $n$ is even, $P(-x)=x^n-ax^{n-1}+\cdots$ and $P(-2x-1)=(2x+1)^n-a(2x+1)^{n-1}+\cdots=2^nx^n+2^{n-1}(n-a)x^{n-1}+\cdots$. The coefficient of $x^{2n-1}$ in $P(-x)P(-2x-1)$ is $2^{n-1}(n-a)-2^na$.

Equating: $2^na+2^{n-1}n+2^{n-1}a=2^{n-1}n-2^{n-1}a-2^na$, i.e. $3\cdot2^na=0$, so $a=0$. The polynomial $P(x)=x^{2016}$ satisfies the identity (it is even), so $a_{2015}=0$ is attained, and it is the only possible value. The sum of all possible values is $0$.

**Answer: 0**

pumac-2016-team-14.title: Root multiplicities
pumac-2016-team-14.body:
Let $m(z)$ be the multiplicity of $z$ as a root of $P$ and $d(z)=m(z)-m(-z)$. Comparing multiplicities of each root $z$ on the two sides gives $d(z)+d(2z+1)=0$. If $d(z)\ne0$ then $d$ is nonzero along the infinite orbit $z\mapsto2z+1$ (unless $z=-1$, where $d(-1)=0$ by oddness), contradicting finiteness. So $d\equiv0$, the roots are symmetric about $0$, and their sum $-a_{2015}$ is $0$.

**Answer: 0**

pumac-2016-team-15.title: Split modulo 32, 9 and 7
pumac-2016-team-15.body:
$2016=32\cdot9\cdot7$, so the number of solutions is the product of the counts mod $32$, mod $9$, mod $7$.

Mod $7$ and mod $9$: the units form cyclic groups of order $6$ ($\{1,3,3^2,\dots\}$ mod 7; $\{1,2,2^2,\dots\}$ mod 9), and $x^n=1$ has $\gcd(n,6)$ solutions in each.

Mod $32$: the units are $\{3^k,5\cdot3^k:0\le k\le7\}$ ($\mathbb Z_8\times\mathbb Z_2$-like structure), with $1$ element of order $1$, $3$ of order $2$, $4$ of order $4$, $8$ of order $8$. So the count is $1,4,8,16$ when $n$ is odd, $\equiv2\pmod4$, $\equiv4\pmod 8$, $\equiv0\pmod8$ respectively.

The total is $\gcd(n,6)^2\cdot c_{32}(n)$ with $c_{32}\in\{1,4,8,16\}$, which must equal $n$. So $n=2^k3^m$. The $3$-part: $\gcd(n,3)^2=3^m$ forces $m\in\{0,2\}$. The $2$-part: $\gcd(n,2)^2c_{32}$ equals $1,16,32,64$ for $n$ odd, $\equiv2\pmod4$, $\equiv4\pmod8$, $\equiv0\pmod8$; this equals the $2$-part $2^k$ of $n$ only for $k=0$ (odd $n$) and $k=6$ ($64$, with $8\mid n$). Checking: $n=1,9,64,576$ all work ($576=16\cdot36$). The sum is $(1+9)(1+64)=650$ (confirmed by brute force).

**Answer: 650**
